strengths: The generate-then-compose formulation addresses a useful problem: preserving independently manipulable, high-quality meshes while recovering their object-object spatial relationship.
The pipeline is intuitively motivated and combines 2D/3D generative priors, robust registration, collision-aware SDF optimization, and semantic refinement in a coherent training-free system.
Qualitative results cover varied object pairs and some multi-object scenes. The rendered examples generally show strong asset fidelity and plausible arrangements compared with the selected baselines.
The quantitative results on the reported ten cases favor Interact3D for both CLIP alignment and intersection metrics, with notably lower surface-intersection ratios.
The paper clearly illustrates the workflow, includes multi-view results and failure cases, and identifies genuine limitations involving symmetry, occlusion, and fine-grained joints.
The proposed dataset of approximately 8,300 compositional scenes could be useful if released with sufficient annotations, provenance, licensing, and quality validation.
weaknesses: Using the default Algorithms/General framing, the empirical evidence is far too limited for the breadth of the claims: quantitative evaluation contains only ten cases, reports only averages, and provides no variance, confidence intervals, category breakdown, systematic sampling protocol, or large-scale success rate.

Claims of producing “physically-sound” and “interactive” assets are not adequately established. Intersection reduction alone does not test contact, support, stability, containment, articulation, mass or material properties, dynamics, or usability in a physics simulator or robot-learning task. The reported intersection values also remain nonzero.

No component ablations isolate the benefits of global-to-local registration, anchor selection, scale-aware ICP, the SDF loss, its continuation schedule, or agentic refinement. The agentic loop is supported mainly by two visual anecdotes, with no success rate, iteration distribution, failure rate, or comparison against non-agentic alternatives.

The baseline study is weak and partly mismatched. Jigsaw targets fractured-object assembly, while 2BY2 is distribution-specific; the highly relevant COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE method is discussed but not evaluated. Moreover, the paper explicitly notes that two learned baselines do not optimize scale, creating an important capability mismatch.

The semantic evaluation may favor the proposed method because its CLIP target is the same Nano Banana Pro image used to construct its spatial guidance. This does not cleanly measure fidelity to an independent ground truth, and no human perceptual study or ground-truth pose benchmark is provided.

The dataset contribution is insufficiently documented and evaluated. Beyond approximate counts, the manuscript omits scene-category distributions, generation and filtering criteria, quality-control procedures, duplicate analysis, train/validation/test splits, mesh validity statistics, failure rates, data provenance, and licensing. No dataset baseline or downstream utility experiment is presented.

Reproducibility is poor because central components rely on proprietary Nano Banana Pro and Gemini 3 Pro services, while prompts, model versions/settings, costs, runtimes, random seeds, and detailed stopping criteria are incomplete. The abstract also contains an unfinished code-release statement.

Several technical details are underspecified: rotation and scale parameterization during optimization, differentiable SDF construction and resolution, point sampling, treatment of non-watertight meshes, correspondence rejection, multi-object collision handling, and convergence criteria. The definition and implementation of “intersected surface area” also need clarification because generic triangle-surface intersections are curves rather than surface regions.

The method is largely an integration of existing generators, PartField, GeoTransformer, ICP, SDF penalties, and a VLM editing loop. The integration is practical, but without stronger ablations and evaluation, the degree of algorithmic originality and generality is not yet convincing.

The paper acknowledges failures from symmetry and erroneous guidance, but does not quantify them. Sequential multi-object composition may accumulate errors and currently has only a few favorable qualitative demonstrations.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear, modular training-free pipeline that combines image-guided asset generation, global-to-local registration, SDF-based collision refinement, and VLM-guided regeneration. Preserving the user-provided mesh while independently generating a complementary asset is practically useful and avoids the holes and fidelity loss shown for direct scene segmentation.
The qualitative examples cover varied object relationships, including containment, support, hanging, insertion, and compositions involving more than two objects.
The proposed dataset of approximately 8,300 compositions could be valuable if its quality, provenance, annotations, and release are established convincingly.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the experimental evidence is substantially inadequate. All quantitative conclusions come from only ten test cases, apparently selected by the authors, with no systematic test-set construction, uncertainty estimates, repeated generations, human evaluation, or evaluation on an established benchmark. This is insufficient to support claims of robustness, generalization, or consistent physical plausibility.

The comparisons are not well controlled. Jigsaw targets fractured-object assembly, while 2BY2 is used without released weights and is trained by the authors; both receive less informative inputs than the proposed pipeline. The closely related COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE work is cited but not evaluated. PartField is not itself a composition method, so its comparison mainly demonstrates a predictable weakness of direct segmentation rather than superiority over a competitive solution.

There are no component ablations for OBB initialization, GeoTransformer, ICP, the SDF loss, its scheduling, anchor selection, or agentic refinement. In particular, the paper never quantifies how often the VLM loop is invoked, how much it improves collision metrics, how often it fails, or whether simpler regeneration strategies perform similarly.

The terms “physically-sound” and “interactive” are overstated. Evaluation measures only mesh interpenetration and CLIP similarity; it does not test support stability, gravity, contact quality, object containment, articulation, dynamics, affordances, or downstream robotic manipulation. Residual collision also remains nonzero. The output appears to be static meshes and poses rather than an interactive simulation asset with physical properties.

Several technical definitions are incomplete or questionable. Vertex-sampled SDF penalties can miss face-level intersections; SDF and inside/outside tests require assumptions about mesh watertightness that are not discussed; transformation constraints and optimization details are underspecified; and “surface area involved in triangle-triangle intersections” is ambiguous because generic triangle intersections have zero area unless the metric instead counts entire intersecting regions or triangles. These omissions hinder verification and reproducibility.

The agentic loop may alter the requested content rather than merely repair geometry—for example, shortening flower branches or changing a teddy bear from sitting to standing. The paper provides no metric for semantic drift, no formal acceptance criterion, and no evidence that a VLM can reliably diagnose hidden internal collisions from the supplied renderings.

The dataset contribution is insufficiently documented. Beyond approximate scene counts, the paper omits source-asset provenance and licensing, prompt/category distributions, quality-control procedures, rejection rates, duplicate analysis, annotation validation, train/validation/test splits, physical metadata, and quantitative dataset statistics. A future release promise alone does not make the dataset independently assessable.

Reproducibility is weak because the pipeline depends heavily on proprietary and changing services such as Nano Banana Pro and Gemini 3 Pro, while prompts, model/API versions, sampling settings, seeds, runtime, monetary cost, hardware, and complete implementation details are not reported.

The methodological novelty is limited: the core system largely connects existing image editing, 3D generation, segmentation, registration, ICP, and SDF optimization components. Pipeline integration may still be useful, but the very small and weakly controlled evaluation does not establish enough empirical significance to compensate. Overall, the work has visible practical promise, but consequential evidence and reproducibility gaps favor rejection.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than purely Algorithms/General: its main value is the effective integration of image editing, 3D generation, segmentation, registration, collision optimization, and VLM-guided refinement into a useful training-free pipeline. Under that framing, the contribution is relevant and potentially impactful.

The generate-then-compose insight is compelling: a monolithic generated scene supplies object-object spatial guidance, while separately generated meshes preserve independent, higher-quality geometry. This directly addresses an important limitation of current image-to-3D systems.

The global-to-local alignment followed by SDF-based collision refinement is technically sensible and modular. The agentic loop further handles geometry incompatibilities that cannot be corrected through rigid transformations alone.

The reported quantitative results consistently favor Interact3D: text CLIP improves from 0.3129 to 0.3307 over the strongest listed baseline, image CLIP from 0.8082 to 0.8248, surface intersection from 2.1523 to 0.6766 times 10^-3, and volume intersection from 6.7744 to 3.2467 times 10^-3.

Qualitative results cover varied relationships such as insertion, support, containment, hanging, and multi-object placement. The multi-view renderings are useful, and the paper candidly illustrates failures involving symmetry, occlusion, and erroneous generative priors.
The proposed dataset of approximately 8,300 compositions, including about 600 scenes with three to five objects, could be a valuable resource if released with adequate metadata and quality control.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evaluation contains only 10 test cases, with no explanation of random sampling, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or human perceptual assessment. This is too small to substantiate broad claims of robust generalization, particularly given the stochastic generative components and the much larger claimed dataset.

There are no component ablations for OBB initialization, GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, the SDF loss and its schedule, or agentic refinement. Consequently, the evidence does not establish which components are necessary, how often the VLM loop succeeds, or how much it improves aggregate performance.

The terms “physically sound” and “interactive” overstate what is demonstrated. The method primarily reduces mesh interpenetration; it does not evaluate gravity, stability, support, contact realism, articulation, mass or friction, collision proxies, or successful use in a physics simulator or robotic learning task.

The collision objective is asymmetric and evaluated on sampled vertices of the remaining mesh against the anchor SDF. It may miss face-level intersections, containment configurations, or collisions in thin and non-watertight geometry. Residual intersection also remains in the reported results.

CLIP agreement with the generated guidance image is limited evidence of correct 3D composition and may favor the proposed method because that same image supplies its spatial target. Contact accuracy, pose error against ground truth, completion quality, and human judgments would provide a more convincing evaluation.

The comparison omits a direct evaluation against COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE despite identifying it as a closely related zero-shot, vision-language-guided composition method. Details needed to assess the fairness and reproducibility of the scratch-trained 2BY2 baseline are also sparse.

The dataset contribution is insufficiently documented: there is no systematic quality audit, success or rejection rate, category distribution, train/test protocol, annotation specification, licensing analysis, or evaluation of errors inherited from the generation pipeline.

Reproducibility is weakened by reliance on proprietary Nano Banana Pro and Gemini 3 Pro services without precise model versions, full system prompts, sampling settings, cost, latency, or determinism analysis. Runtime and computational requirements for the complete pipeline are not reported, and the manuscript contains an incomplete code-release statement.

Overall, the system is promising and visually convincing enough for a borderline acceptance, but the recommendation is held back by the very limited quantitative sample, absence of ablations, and mismatch between collision avoidance and the stronger physical-validity claims.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/8db5a226ef3442b4946945a631e7ea0e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a useful computer-vision and robotics problem: generating independently manipulable 3D objects while preserving their intended spatial relationships, instead of producing one fused scene mesh.

The central generate-then-compose idea is practical and intuitive: a generated scene supplies coarse 3D spatial guidance, while separately generated meshes preserve object completeness and appearance. The combination of robust registration, collision-aware refinement, and semantic regeneration handles several failure modes of direct segmentation.

Results are visually appealing and cover varied object pairs, multi-object scenes, failure cases, and six-view renderings. The paper also provides quantitative comparisons and a component ablation over 150 cases; the reported improvements are consistent across semantic ratings and penetration metrics.
The paper is generally well organized, and the figures communicate the workflow effectively. It explicitly acknowledges symmetry, occlusion, reconstruction, and fine-component limitations.
The proposed collection of roughly 8,300 compositional scenes could be valuable if released with sufficiently complete provenance, metadata, quality control, and licensing documentation.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the algorithmic novelty is modest. Most components—commercial image editing/VLM services, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer, ICP, and an SDF penalty—are existing techniques assembled into a pipeline. The integration is useful, but the experimental evidence must therefore be especially rigorous to establish a substantial scientific contribution.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified. The manuscript does not explain how the 150 test cases were sampled, whether they overlap with the 8,300-scene dataset or development examples, how prompts and reference meshes were selected, or whether failures were excluded during curation. Figure 7 reports 29 failures among 140 additional cases (about 21%) while describing them as only a small fraction, and no formal success-rate metric is given.

Human evaluation lacks the number and identity/qualification of raters, instructions, blinding and randomization procedures, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty, or statistical testing. The Qwen3 evaluator similarly lacks its exact variant, prompt, rendering inputs, decoding configuration, and repeated-trial analysis. Consequently, the large rating advantages in Tables 2 and 3 are difficult to verify.

Baseline comparability is questionable. Jigsaw, 2BY2, and MIDI were developed for materially different input settings or training distributions, whereas Interact3D receives strong proprietary image-generation and VLM priors. The closely related zero-shot COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE method is discussed but not evaluated. There are also no comparisons with the claimed segmentation/inpainting capabilities of Hunyuan3D or Rodin, and no oracle or simple optimization baseline that uses equivalent generated guidance.

The claim of producing “physically-sound” or interactive assets is substantially stronger than the evidence. The method evaluates interpenetration only; it does not test contact stability, gravity, support, friction, mass properties, articulation, dynamics, simulator compatibility, or downstream robotic manipulation. Several showcased relationships may be collision-light yet physically unstable.

The geometric evaluation is not adequately defined. Triangle intersections ordinarily form curves rather than surface regions, so the computation of “intersected surface area” needs a precise algorithm. The volume test assumes reliable inside/outside classification even though generated or segmented meshes can contain holes. There is no robustness analysis for mesh resolution, SDF discretization, sampling variance, or thin structures, and a vertex-sampled collision loss can miss face-face intersections.

Reproducibility is presently weak. The paper omits the SDF construction and resolution, point-sampling strategy, optimizer and learning rates, detailed schedules, registration thresholds, canonical-camera definition, VLM prompts, stopping detector, random seeds, per-stage runtime, API cost, and failure/retry policy. Dependence on Nano Banana Pro and Gemini 3 Pro also introduces proprietary and mutable components; the code and dataset URLs are blank promises rather than available artifacts.

The dataset description is too sparse to evaluate the dataset contribution: it provides no asset provenance or licenses, prompt-generation process, per-category statistics, filtering criteria for reducing 10,000 candidates to 8,300 scenes, train/validation/test splits, quality annotations, duplicate analysis, physical metadata, or quantitative audit. These omissions are especially important because the paper motivates the resource for robotic simulation.

The agentic ablation is not fully controlled: regenerating geometry can change appearance and semantics as well as resolve collisions, while CLIP and rating metrics are tied to images produced by the same generative ecosystem. The paper should report invocation frequency, iterations, success rate, regressions, cost, and paired results specifically on cases that trigger refinement.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: generating separate, geometrically compatible 3D assets is useful for scene construction and potentially for simulation, while preserving a user-provided mesh avoids the damage caused by segmenting a fused generated scene.

The generate-then-compose pipeline is intuitive and clearly organized. Combining spatial guidance, global-to-local registration, an SDF collision term, and semantic regeneration provides a practical way to handle increasingly difficult failures.

The submission includes 150-case quantitative evaluation, component ablations, multi-view visualizations, and explicit failure cases. These are useful additions, and the reported results consistently favor the complete pipeline.

The proposed collection of approximately 8,300 compositions could become a useful resource if its assets, metadata, construction procedure, licenses, and quality controls are fully documented and released.
The paper is generally readable, and the figures communicate the overall workflow and qualitative improvements effectively.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess the work as Algorithms/General. Viewed instead as an Applied/Systems paper, the integration would be more appropriate, but the central physical-validity and reproducibility deficiencies would still prevent acceptance. Algorithmic originality is limited: most of the pipeline combines Nano Banana Pro, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer, ICP, a conventional SDF penalty, and a VLM editing loop.

The experimental comparison is not sufficiently fair or comprehensive. Interact3D uses generated scene guidance, text/image information, proprietary image editing, and VLM feedback, whereas Jigsaw and 2BY2 receive only the two meshes. Several baselines are trained for substantially different domains. The closely related COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE method is discussed but not evaluated, and the direct PartField baseline is omitted from all quantitative metrics.

The claim of producing “physically-sound” or simulation-ready interactive scenes is substantially overstated. Evaluation measures only semantic similarity and geometric intersection. There are no tests of support, gravity, stability, contact quality, dynamics, manipulability, or downstream simulation/robot-learning utility. Separate collision-reduced meshes are not by themselves interactive assets, particularly without physical parameters, articulation, or collision proxies.

The collision metrics are inadequately defined and potentially unreliable. Triangle-triangle intersections generally form curves rather than surface regions with area, so the definition of A_int requires a precise implementation. The volume metric assumes meaningful inside/outside tests on solid meshes even though the paper repeatedly notes holes and reconstruction artifacts. Neither metric is accompanied by robustness checks or validation against manually assessed collisions.

The SDF loss is asymmetric and apparently evaluated only at vertices of the remaining mesh. It can miss edge-face intersections, configurations where the anchor is contained in the remaining object, and collisions between sparsely sampled surfaces. Its repulsion term can also favor gaps or floating objects. SDF resolution, mesh preprocessing, sampling, optimization details, and handling of non-watertight meshes are missing.

Evaluation methodology is under-specified. The paper does not report the number of human raters, rating instructions, blinding/randomization, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty, or significance tests. The exact CLIP and Qwen3 variants, prompts, rendering viewpoints, aggregation protocol, and repeated-run variability are also absent. Consequently, the large human/VLM score differences in Tables 2 and 3 are difficult to audit.

The test-set construction and independence are unclear. The 150 cases include displayed cases, but there is no sampling protocol, held-out split, category breakdown, or protection against selection bias. Figure 7 itself reports 29 failures among 140 additional cases—about 21%, despite describing them as a “small fraction”—which indicates a substantial failure rate that is not reflected in aggregate reporting.

The dataset contribution is not adequately substantiated. Only coarse category and object-count statistics are supplied; the manuscript omits asset provenance, licensing, prompt generation, filtering criteria, duplicate analysis, train/test splits, annotation validation, quality measurements, and comparison with existing datasets. The stated code-and-dataset availability line also provides no usable link.

Reproducibility is poor because essential stages depend on proprietary and evolving Google models. Exact model versions, API parameters, seeds, full system/editing prompts, retry policy, costs, latency, and failure handling are not documented. TRELLIS2/PartField settings and the from-scratch 2BY2 training protocol are likewise insufficiently specified.

The agentic refinement ablation is confounded: it regenerates the complementary geometry rather than isolating pose refinement, and evaluation against an image produced by the same image-generation ecosystem may favor this loop. There is no comparison to simpler retry, rule-based editing, direct collision feedback, or non-agentic regeneration strategies.

The multi-object extension is demonstrated mainly through a few qualitative examples. Sequential composition can accumulate registration errors and creates collisions involving a growing, potentially non-watertight anchor, but scaling behavior, success rate versus object count, runtime, model-call count, and computational cost are not evaluated.

Overall, the pipeline is promising as a systems prototype, but inadequate validation, unfair baseline information, limited reproducibility, and overclaiming of physical soundness are consequential shortcomings. The balance therefore favors a weak reject rather than acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a useful Algorithms/General contribution with a systems component: generated 3D scenes are used as spatial guidance while independently generated, higher-quality meshes are retained as final assets. This generate-then-compose formulation is practical and addresses a meaningful limitation of monolithic 3D generation and direct part segmentation.

The pipeline is technically coherent. Global-to-local registration addresses partial overlap and initialization sensitivity, the SDF objective explicitly reduces interpenetration, and the VLM-guided loop can modify geometry when rigid pose optimization is insufficient. The ablation study supports each stage, with the full system improving semantic ratings and reducing surface and volume intersection ratios.

The empirical results are broadly favorable. Across 150 cases, the method substantially outperforms the reported baselines in CLIP similarity, human/VLM ratings, and both collision metrics. The numerous qualitative and multi-view examples show diverse object relationships, preservation of individual asset quality, and extension beyond two-object composition.

The proposed dataset of approximately 8,300 scenes—substantially larger than the cited 2BY2 collection—could be valuable to compositional generation and robotics research. The manuscript is generally clear, visually effective, and candid about symmetry, occlusion, and fine-grained-component failures.
weaknesses: The claim of producing "physically sound" or "physically plausible" interactive scenes is stronger than the evidence. The evaluation measures geometric interpenetration, but not support, stability under gravity, contact quality, articulation, mass or friction properties, or performance in a physics simulator or manipulation task. The paper should frame its validated contribution more narrowly as collision-aware geometric composition unless such tests are added.

Important evaluation details are missing: the number and recruitment of human raters, rating instructions, inter-rater agreement, the exact Qwen model and prompting protocol, uncertainty or statistical significance, and per-category results. Figure 7 also reports 29 failures among 140 cases, about 21%, which is not obviously a "small fraction" and warrants a clearer success criterion and breakdown.

Baseline coverage and fairness could be stronger. Jigsaw, 2BY2, and MIDI were developed for related but materially different settings, and some are intentionally evaluated without the image/text signals available to the proposed pipeline. The highly relevant COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE method is discussed but not compared, while the direct PartField baseline is omitted from quantitative geometric evaluation.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on proprietary, evolving Nano Banana Pro and Gemini services. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify model/API versions, decoding settings, complete system prompts, optimization solver and rotation parameterization, runtime and monetary cost, or stopping decisions for the agentic loop. The promised code and dataset URL is also absent in the submitted version.

The dataset contribution needs more documentation before its value can be fully assessed: the source and licensing of reference meshes, prompt-generation procedure, acceptance criteria for filtering roughly 10,000 candidates to 8,300 scenes, train/test separation, duplicate control, and systematic quality validation are not provided. More broadly, the algorithmic novelty lies mainly in the integration of existing generators, PartField, GeoTransformer/ICP, SDF penalties, and VLM editing rather than a fundamentally new component.
